title: HMRC’s child benefit travel-data intervention: what went wrong, what was fixed, and what’s next
label: 29 October 2026 · HMRC child benefit data intervention
summary: The Committee examined HMRC’s 2025 use of Home Office travel data to find people who might be claiming child benefit after leaving the UK. HMRC accept the National Audit Office’s criticisms: changes made when moving from pilot to first roll-out caused unnecessary suspensions of legitimate payments. HMRC apologised, reinstated most payments, accepted NAO recommendations, introduced stricter oversight, a ‘hypercare’ phase and simplified customer steps. The witnesses set out what happened, why mistakes were made, how they fixed them, and how lessons will be shared across Government.

glossary.definition: Records of people entering and leaving the UK used to see if claimants had traveled abroad.
Pay As You Earn—HMRC’s regular tax information from employers used to check if someone is working in the UK.
A careful, slow-scale phase after a pilot where every case and customer contact is closely checked.
The law that allows government departments to share data for public service and fraud prevention, under rules and oversight.

chapters.title: What the intervention was and HMRC’s opening admission
chapters.takeaway: HMRC used travel data to find likely ineligible child benefit claims, apologised after the first roll-out caused harm, and accepted NAO recommendations.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Child benefit supports millions and cost £13.3bn in 2024–25. HMRC used Home Office travel data in 2025 to find people who may have moved abroad and were no longer eligible.

turns.speaker: John-Paul Marks
turns.text: We accept the NAO’s findings and have accepted all recommendations. The pilot showed strong results, but the first roll-out made mistakes. I apologised to affected customers, we reinstated payments and offered redress.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: The pilot seemed to work: six in 10 flagged claims were in error. But decisions changed in roll-out—removing an upfront PAYE check and altering forms—and that’s where things went wrong. Who authorised those changes?

turns.speaker: John-Paul Marks
turns.text: I’m accountable as HMRC chief executive. Those operational changes were made to scale quickly, but they were outside our risk tolerance. We reversed the changes, put PAYE checks back, added a grace period and simplified evidence requirements.

turns.speaker: Rob Malcomson
turns.text: The pilot was successful but highlights the need for guardrails. The Digital Economy Act review board and the PSFA will use this learning across Government.

chapters.title: Pilot to roll-out: how the changes caused harm
chapters.takeaway: Changes made when scaling up—especially removing checks and asking for too much evidence—led to thousands of eligible claimants having payments suspended.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: The NAO said key decisions were made at inappropriate levels. Were there minutes of the workshop where this happened, and who is responsible going forward?

turns.speaker: John-Paul Marks
turns.text: I will check the paperwork, but operational teams acted to scale innovation. Now Myrtle’s directorate runs the business-as-usual process and Cerys is the policy owner—there’s clearer senior accountability.

turns.speaker: Sarah Olney
turns.text: You described the disruption as a 'bump in the road'. For families, paused child benefit can mean real hardship. Why was customer impact not considered when those roll-out changes were made?

turns.speaker: John-Paul Marks
turns.text: No intent to cause harm. It was poor judgement to scale without re-testing at volume. We paused when problems were spotted, reinstated payments, apologised and offered redress.

turns.speaker: Myrtle Lloyd
turns.text: From pilot to scale we added a 'hypercare' phase: when we now roll out we do close follow-up calls, 100% quality checks and watch colleague capability so customers aren’t left without help.

turns.speaker: Sarah Olney
turns.text: Forms initially asked for up to 73 items including school or GP letters. That was disproportionate. Have those requirements changed?

turns.speaker: Myrtle Lloyd
turns.text: Yes. We reduced the questions to about 15 and now ask for two pieces of evidence—return travel and bank transactions—submitted digitally where possible.

chapters.title: Scale of impact, reinstatement and redress
chapters.takeaway: About 9,000 ineligible claims were stopped saving £50m, but thousands of eligible claimants were suspended; most payments were reinstated quickly and redress offered, though compensation paid was small.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: You stopped around 9,000 people who were ineligible, saving over £50m, yet 61% of the initial 23,794 inquiries were actually eligible. That’s a high false-positive rate.

turns.speaker: John-Paul Marks
turns.text: The pilot non-compliance rate was ~60%. First roll-out was lower—about 38–39%—because of the changes we later reversed. In hypercare more recently, non-compliance rose again closer to pilot levels.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: NAO said 40% of eligible claimants were automatically reinstated by November 2025, but HMRC couldn't provide average reinstatement time. Can you supply the range?

turns.speaker: John-Paul Marks
turns.text: Yes—broadly the roll-out ran August–October, we paused and fixed by the end of November. Worst cases from August waited around three months. We'll write with fuller ranges and timings.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You paid £3,200 to 51 claimants—small sums overall. Were you making it hard to claim compensation, and do you pay interest on late payments?

turns.speaker: Myrtle Lloyd
turns.text: We tried not to put barriers in the way. The payments were small because most people were reinstated and backdated promptly. The largest single redress was £300.

turns.speaker: Sarah Olney
turns.text: Can you confirm no one lost state pension entitlement because of suspensions?

turns.speaker: Cerys McDonald
turns.text: Yes—suspension did not terminate entitlement. Based on current information I can give the Committee an undertaking that state pension entitlement wasn’t affected; I will write if anything changes.

chapters.title: Governance, accountability and cross‑Government lessons
chapters.takeaway: HMRC accepts it lacked sufficient senior oversight in the move to scale; it has implemented internal audit and NAO recommendations and is sharing lessons across Government via the Public Sector Fraud Authority.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: NAO highlighted absence of a continuous senior responsible owner. Was that lacking here and has it been fixed?

turns.speaker: John-Paul Marks
turns.text: Yes, NAO was right—SRO presence was insufficient in that phase. We’ve accepted the recommendation and now have clearer senior ownership, oversight and governance for scaling.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: You commissioned an internal audit—will you share its findings?

turns.speaker: John-Paul Marks
turns.text: Yes. The internal audit informed our action plan and has been shared with the NAO and our audit committees. We’ll share outcomes as part of accountability.

turns.speaker: Rob Malcomson
turns.text: This is broadly an isolated incident but instructive. The Digital Economy Act review board, the PSFA and a community of practice will push hypercare and pre-deployment guardrails across Departments.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Athow
turns.text: We discussed the lessons at HMRC’s professional standards committee in 2026 to reassure colleagues we can innovate safely; we will use that governance route going forward.

turns.speaker: Mr Betts
turns.text: How do you stop staff becoming overly risk-averse after this?

turns.speaker: John-Paul Marks
turns.text: We want a high appetite for responsible innovation—empowerment plus clear guardrails and senior oversight. The risk is lowering ambition; instead we aim for disciplined, tested scaling with customer safeguards.

turns.speaker: Rob Malcomson
turns.text: Bring policy, operations, legal and data governance together at design stage—co-design reduces surprises and allows safe innovation.

chapters.title: Next steps: data sources, debt recovery and public trust
chapters.takeaway: HMRC will expand safe data use (student, schools, other travel data), proceed cautiously with new debt powers, and commit to more transparency and monitoring to maintain public trust.

turns.speaker: Catherine West
turns.text: What additional data sources and nudges will HMRC use to spot changes in entitlement and latent unmet need?

turns.speaker: Cerys McDonald
turns.text: We already use school census, Student Loans Company and DWP feeds; we’ll add more targeted nudges (texts to parents) and use feeds to spot education or benefit claims changes quickly.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Should claimants confirm eligibility annually?

turns.speaker: John-Paul Marks
turns.text: We balance burden on 7 million families with targeted checks. There is already reconfirmation around age 16; we’ll improve nudges and tech to reduce burden while catching riskier cohorts.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: About debt: the Chancellor announced powers for direct deductions. That’s draconian—how will you safeguard people before using it?

turns.speaker: John-Paul Marks
turns.text: We’ll write to the Committee before December. Direct deduction will be a last resort, tested at low volume with senior oversight, refund-first safeguards and published controls to protect cashflow for vulnerable people.

turns.speaker: Rob Malcomson
turns.text: Better data quality—uniform identifiers and property/ residency data—would make these checks more accurate. Where data gaps remain, probabilistic matching plus follow-up contact must be used, not automatic action.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. The Committee will follow up for detailed timelines, reinstatement ranges, the internal audit outcomes and the promised letter on direct deduction safeguards.
